statement: Let $M$ be a closed orientable [3-manifold](c:3-manifold). Cut $M$ along finitely many disjoint embedded 2-spheres and cap the boundary with balls. Cut each irreducible piece along finitely many incompressible tori. The interior of each final piece has a complete finite-volume metric modeled on one of the eight [Thurston geometries](c:thurston-geometry).

hypotheses.text: $M$ is a closed orientable [3-manifold](c:3-manifold).

conclusion: The pieces of the decomposition are geometric: each interior carries a complete finite-volume metric of one of the eight [Thurston geometries](c:thurston-geometry).

proofs.name: Ricci flow with surgery
proofs.slogan: Run [Ricci flow](c:ricci-flow) with surgery from a metric on $M$ and read the decomposition from the extinct and long-time behavior of the flow.
proofs.scope: An outline of Perelman's proof as completed by Morgan and Tian; each step rests on the cited work. It proves existence of the decomposition; uniqueness is the older Kneser-Milnor and Jaco-Shalen-Johannson theory.

roles.why: A closed orientable $M$ carries metrics, and the flow with surgery stays among closed orientable 3-manifolds.

steps.slogan: Start Ricci flow with surgery from a metric on $M$.
steps.detail: Perelman's [Ricci flow](c:ricci-flow) with surgery cuts along small 2-spheres near singularities and caps the cuts with balls. It exists for all time and does not collapse locally at bounded scale, by his entropy monotonicity. The cut spheres give the [connected sum](c:connected-sum) decomposition of $M$.

steps.slogan: Handle finite-time extinction, which leaves only spherical space forms and copies of $S^2 \times S^1$.
steps.detail: When $\pi_1(M)$ is a free product of finite and infinite cyclic groups, the flow dies in finite time (Perelman; Colding and Minicozzi). Every prime summand is then a spherical space form or $S^2 \times S^1$, which are geometric.

steps.slogan: Split the long-time flow into a thick hyperbolic part and a thin collapsed part.
steps.detail: If the flow lives for all time, rescale the metrics to bounded size. Hamilton and Perelman show that the thick part converges to finite-volume [hyperbolic 3-manifolds](c:hyperbolic-3-manifold) with cusps, and its boundary tori are incompressible in $M$.

steps.slogan: Show that the thin collapsed part is a graph manifold with incompressible boundary tori.
steps.detail: Perelman's collapsing theory gives curvature bounded below on the thin part. Morgan and Tian glue local models from Alexandrov spaces to show that this part is a graph manifold, a union of Seifert pieces glued along tori.

steps.slogan: Assemble hyperbolic, Seifert and Sol pieces along incompressible tori into the geometric decomposition.
steps.detail: Cut the graph manifold along its tori into [Seifert fibered](c:seifert-fibration) pieces and torus bundles; they carry the six non-hyperbolic geometries. With the hyperbolic pieces and the spherical case, every piece of $M$ has one of the eight geometries.

concepts.c:3-manifold: The theorem classifies the pieces of a closed orientable 3-manifold.
concepts.c:thurston-geometry: The eight geometries are the possible models of the final pieces.
concepts.c:ricci-flow: Ricci flow with surgery is the tool that produces the decomposition.
concepts.c:connected-sum: Surgery spheres recover the sphere decomposition of the manifold.
concepts.c:hyperbolic-3-manifold: The thick part of the long-time flow gives the hyperbolic pieces.
concepts.c:seifert-fibration: The graph manifold part splits into Seifert fibered pieces.

source.ref: J. Morgan and G. Tian, Completion of the proof of the Geometrization Conjecture, arXiv:0809.4040 (2008); building on G. Perelman, arXiv:math/0211159, math/0303109, math/0307245, and Morgan and Tian, Ricci Flow and the Poincare Conjecture, Clay Mathematics Monographs 3, AMS, 2007
source.note: The five steps follow the published proof: Ricci flow with surgery, finite extinction, the thick-thin decomposition, the collapsed part as a graph manifold, and the assembly of the pieces.

statement: Let $v_1, \dots, v_n$ be vectors of an [inner product space](c:inner-product-space). Set $u_k = v_k - \sum_{j<k} c_{jk} u_j$, where $c_{jk} = \langle u_j, v_k\rangle / \langle u_j, u_j\rangle$, and drop the term when $u_j = 0$. Then the $u_k$ are pairwise orthogonal, and $u_1, \dots, u_k$ span the same space as $v_1, \dots, v_k$ for each $k$.

hypotheses.text: The vectors lie in an [inner product space](c:inner-product-space) over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$.
The family $v_1, \dots, v_n$ is finite and ordered.

conclusion: The $u_k$ are pairwise [orthogonal](c:orthogonality), and $\operatorname{span}(u_1, \dots, u_k) = \operatorname{span}(v_1, \dots, v_k)$ for every $k$.

formal.difference: The declaration proves orthogonality only, for a well-ordered locally finite index set. The span statement is the separate declaration span_gramSchmidt_Iic.

proofs.name: Induction on the index
proofs.slogan: Subtract from each vector its [projections](c:orthogonal-projection) on the earlier ones and check, by induction on the index, that the result is orthogonal to all earlier vectors.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, with the inner product linear in the second slot. Zero vectors $u_j$ are allowed: their term is dropped, and orthogonality to them is trivial.

roles.why: The inner product defines the projection coefficients and the orthogonality of two vectors.
Finitely many predecessors make the recursion well founded and allow induction on the index.

steps.slogan: Define $u_k$ by subtracting from $v_k$ its projections on the earlier $u_j$.
steps.detail: Let $P_j x = c\, u_j$ with $c = \langle u_j, x\rangle / \langle u_j, u_j\rangle$ be the [orthogonal projection](c:orthogonal-projection) on the line of $u_j$, and $P_j = 0$ when $u_j = 0$. Then $u_k = v_k - \sum_{j<k} P_j v_k$. Each $u_k$ uses only earlier $u_j$.

steps.slogan: Fix $k$ and assume that $u_1, \dots, u_{k-1}$ are pairwise orthogonal.
steps.detail: This is strong induction on $k$. For $k = 1$ there is no pair to check, and $u_1 = v_1$.

steps.slogan: Expand $\langle u_a, u_k \rangle$ for $a < k$ by linearity.
steps.detail: Linearity in the second slot gives $\langle u_a, u_k\rangle = \langle u_a, v_k\rangle - \sum_{j<k} c_{jk} \langle u_a, u_j\rangle$.

steps.slogan: Cancel every term with $j \ne a$ by the induction hypothesis, and the term $j = a$ against $\langle u_a, v_k\rangle$.
steps.detail: For $j \ne a$ both indices are below $k$, so $\langle u_a, u_j\rangle = 0$. The term $j = a$ equals $c_{ak}\langle u_a, u_a\rangle = \langle u_a, v_k\rangle$ if $u_a \ne 0$, and both sides are $0$ if $u_a = 0$. Hence $\langle u_a, u_k\rangle = 0$.

steps.slogan: Show by induction that $u_1, \dots, u_k$ and $v_1, \dots, v_k$ span the same space.
steps.detail: The vector $u_k = v_k - \sum_{j<k} c_{jk}u_j$ lies in $\operatorname{span}(v_1, \dots, v_k)$, since $u_j$ with $j<k$ does. Conversely $v_k = u_k + \sum_{j<k} c_{jk}u_j$ lies in $\operatorname{span}(u_1, \dots, u_k)$. So the spans are equal.

steps.slogan: Join orthogonality for $a<k$ with the span equality for every $k$.
steps.detail: Orthogonality is symmetric, so the case $a<k$ covers every pair $a \ne k$. The span equality holds for every $k$ by the previous step.

concepts.c:inner-product-space: The inner product gives the projection coefficients and orthogonality.
concepts.c:orthogonality: Pairwise orthogonality of the $u_k$ is the main claim.
concepts.c:orthogonal-projection: Each subtracted term is the projection of $v_k$ on a line.

source.note: mathlib inducts on the larger index (WellFounded.induction), unfolds gramSchmidt_def, and isolates the term i = a with Finset.sum_eq_single_of_mem; the span step follows span_gramSchmidt_Iic.

statement: For every finite sequence $a_0, \dots, a_{m-1}$ of natural numbers there are natural numbers $p$ and $q$ with $a_i = p \bmod ((i+1)q + 1)$ for every $i < m$. So the pair $(p, q)$ is a [sequence coding](c:sequence-coding) using only [modular arithmetic](c:modular-arithmetic).

hypotheses.text: The sequence $a_0, \dots, a_{m-1}$ is finite, of [natural numbers](c:natural-number), and may be empty.

conclusion: There are $p, q$ with $a_i = p \bmod ((i+1)q+1)$ for all $i < m$.

formal.difference: mathlib packs the pair $(p, q)$ into one number with Nat.pair and defines beta n i by Nat.unpair. The choice of $q$ and the use of the Chinese remainder theorem are the same as here.

proofs.name: Chinese remainder theorem
proofs.slogan: Pick a factorial $q$ that makes the moduli $(i+1)q+1$ pairwise [coprime](c:coprime-integers) and larger than the entries, then solve all congruences at once.
proofs.scope: The whole lemma. For $m = 0$ the system is empty and $p = 0$ works.

roles.why: Finiteness gives a bound for all entries and finitely many congruences to solve.

steps.slogan: Choose $q = s!$ with $s$ larger than $m$ and than every $a_i$.
steps.detail: The sequence is finite, so $s = \max(m, a_0, \dots, a_{m-1}) + 1$ exists. Put $q = s!$.

steps.slogan: Form the moduli $m_i = (i+1)q + 1$ and show that each exceeds $a_i$.
steps.detail: Since $s! \ge s$, we get $m_i \ge s! + 1 > s > a_i$ for every $i < m$.

steps.slogan: Show that the moduli are pairwise coprime.
steps.detail: Let a prime $\ell$ divide $m_i$ and $m_j$ with $i < j < m$. Then $\ell$ divides $m_j - m_i = (j-i)q$. Because $0 < j - i < s$, every prime factor of $j - i$ is at most $s$ and divides $s! = q$, so $\ell \mid q$ in both cases. Then $\ell \mid (i+1)q$ and $\ell \mid m_i - (i+1)q = 1$, a contradiction.

steps.slogan: Solve the system $p \equiv a_i \pmod{m_i}$ for all $i < m$.
steps.detail: The moduli are pairwise coprime, so the Chinese remainder theorem gives a natural number $p$ with $p \equiv a_i \pmod{m_i}$ for every $i<m$.

steps.slogan: Read $a_i$ as the remainder of $p$ modulo $m_i$.
steps.detail: We have $p \equiv a_i \pmod{m_i}$ and $0 \le a_i < m_i$. So $p \bmod m_i = a_i$, that is $a_i = p \bmod ((i+1)q+1)$.

concepts.c:sequence-coding: The pair $(p, q)$ is the code of the whole sequence.
concepts.c:modular-arithmetic: Entries are recovered as remainders modulo the chosen moduli.
concepts.c:natural-number: Entries and codes are natural numbers, which gives bounds and remainders.
concepts.c:coprime-integers: Pairwise coprime moduli are what the Chinese remainder theorem needs.

source.note: mathlib takes supOfSeq, the moduli coprimes a i = (i+1)(sup)!+1, proves pairwise coprimality (coprime_mul_succ) and applies Nat.chineseRemainderOfFinset, then reads off the entry with Nat.mod_eq_of_modEq.

statement: Let $G$ be a finite [graph](c:graph) and $P$ a strictly positive distribution of finitely many variables $X_v$ indexed by its vertices. Then $P$ is a [Markov random field](c:markov-random-field) on $G$ if and only if $P(x) = \prod_C \psi_C(x_C)$ over the [cliques](c:clique) $C$ of $G$, with positive factors $\psi_C$ that depend only on $x_C$.

hypotheses.text: $G = (V, E)$ is a finite [graph](c:graph).
Each variable $X_v$ takes values in a finite set $S_v$.
The distribution satisfies $P(x) > 0$ for every $x \in \prod_v S_v$.

conclusion: $P$ is Markov on $G$ exactly when it is a [Gibbs distribution](c:gibbs-distribution) with positive clique factors.

proofs.name: Möbius inversion over subsets
proofs.slogan: A clique factorization gives the Markov property by cancelling factors; for the converse, expand $\log P$ by Möbius inversion and show that the terms of non-cliques vanish.
proofs.scope: Markov means the local Markov property: $X_v$ is independent of the non-neighbors given the neighbors. For positive $P$ this equals the pairwise and global forms.

roles.why: The graph defines neighbors for the Markov property and the cliques for the factors.
Finite state sets make the sums over states and the substituted states $x^B$ finite and well defined.
Positivity makes the logarithms and the conditional probabilities well defined.

steps.slogan: Show that a clique factorization gives the Markov property.
steps.detail: Fix $v$ and the other coordinates. The conditional probability of $x_v$ is the product of factors containing $v$, divided by its sum over $x_v$; factors without $v$ cancel. Every clique containing $v$ lies in $v$ and its neighbors, so the conditional law depends on the neighbors only.

steps.slogan: Fix a reference state $x^*$ and set $H(x) = \log (P(x)/P(x^*))$.
steps.detail: Positivity makes $H$ defined. For $B \subseteq V$ let $x^B$ agree with $x$ on $B$ and with $x^*$ outside $B$. Then $x^V = x$ and $H(x^\emptyset) = 0$.

steps.slogan: Expand $H$ as a sum $\sum_A \varphi_A(x)$ by Möbius inversion over subsets.
steps.detail: Put $\varphi_A(x) = \sum_{B \subseteq A} (-1)^{|A \setminus B|} H(x^B)$. By inclusion-exclusion, $\sum_{A \subseteq V} \varphi_A(x) = H(x^V) = H(x)$. Each $\varphi_A$ reads only the coordinates in $A$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\varphi_A = 0$ when $A$ is not a clique.
steps.detail: Take non-adjacent $u \ne v$ in $A$ and group the sum over $B \subseteq A \setminus \{u, v\}$ into brackets $H(x^{B \cup \{u,v\}}) - H(x^{B \cup \{u\}}) - H(x^{B \cup \{v\}}) + H(x^B)$. Each bracket is a difference of two log ratios of the conditional law of $X_u$, taken at two states that differ only at $v$. By [conditional independence](c:conditional-independence) of $X_u$ from the non-neighbor $v$, the two ratios agree, so the bracket is $0$.

steps.slogan: Write $P$ as a product of positive clique factors.
steps.detail: Now $P(x) = P(x^*) \exp \sum_{C\ \mathrm{clique}} \varphi_C(x)$. Put $\psi_C = \exp \varphi_C$ and absorb $P(x^*)$ into one factor. Each $\psi_C$ is positive and depends only on $x_C$.

steps.slogan: Join both implications into the stated equivalence.
steps.detail: Step 1 gives factorization implies Markov. Steps 2 to 5 give Markov implies factorization.

concepts.c:graph: Its edges define neighbors and its cliques index the factors.
concepts.c:markov-random-field: The Markov property on the graph is one side of the equivalence.
concepts.c:clique: Only cliques carry nonzero terms in the expansion of $\log P$.
concepts.c:gibbs-distribution: The clique product form is the Gibbs form.
concepts.c:conditional-independence: It kills the mixed second difference for non-adjacent vertices.

source.note: The Möbius inversion proof of Grimmett (1973) and Besag (1974), as presented in Lauritzen, Graphical Models, Oxford University Press, 1996, chapter 3.

statement: Let $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{B}$ be [lower sets](c:lower-set) of subsets of a [finite set](c:finite-set) $X$ with $|X| = n$: [families of sets](c:family-of-sets) closed under taking subsets. Then $|\mathcal{A}|\,|\mathcal{B}| \le 2^n\, |\mathcal{A} \cap \mathcal{B}|$.

hypotheses.text: $X$ is a [finite set](c:finite-set) with $n$ elements.
$\mathcal{A}$ is a [lower set](c:lower-set): $S \in \mathcal{A}$ and $T \subseteq S$ imply $T \in \mathcal{A}$.
$\mathcal{B}$ is a [lower set](c:lower-set) of subsets of $X$.

proofs.name: Induction on the ground set
proofs.slogan: Split both families by one element, compare the four sizes with a two-term Chebyshev inequality, and apply induction to the two halves.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, proved for lower families inside the power set of a set $S$ with $|S| = n$ by induction on $n$. The case $n = 0$ is checked directly.

roles.why: Removing one element lowers $n$ by one, which drives the induction.
Lowness of $\mathcal{A}$ makes both halves lower and gives $\mathcal{A}_1 \subseteq \mathcal{A}_0$.
Lowness of $\mathcal{B}$ makes both halves lower and gives $\mathcal{B}_1 \subseteq \mathcal{B}_0$.

steps.slogan: State the claim for lower families of subsets of any set $S$ of size $n$, and induct on $n$.
steps.detail: Claim: for lower families $\mathcal{A}, \mathcal{B}$ inside the power set of $S$, $|\mathcal{A}||\mathcal{B}| \le 2^{|S|}|\mathcal{A} \cap \mathcal{B}|$. The step from $n-1$ to $n$ removes one element $a \in S$.

steps.slogan: Check the case $n = 0$ by hand.
steps.detail: A lower family of subsets of $\emptyset$ is $\emptyset$ or $\{\emptyset\}$. If one family is empty the left side is $0$. Otherwise both equal $\{\emptyset\}$ and $1 \le 1$.

steps.slogan: Split each family by the element $a$ into two lower families.
steps.detail: Let $\mathcal{A}_0 = \{T \in \mathcal{A} : a \notin T\}$ and $\mathcal{A}_1 = \{T \setminus \{a\} : T \in \mathcal{A}, a \in T\}$, and define $\mathcal{B}_0, \mathcal{B}_1$ alike. Then $|\mathcal{A}| = |\mathcal{A}_0| + |\mathcal{A}_1|$, both are lower families inside the power set of $S \setminus \{a\}$, and $\mathcal{A}_1 \subseteq \mathcal{A}_0$ because $\mathcal{A}$ is lower. The same holds for $\mathcal{B}$.

steps.slogan: Bound the product of the sums by twice the sum of the products.
steps.detail: The difference $2(|\mathcal{A}_0||\mathcal{B}_0| + |\mathcal{A}_1||\mathcal{B}_1|) - (|\mathcal{A}_0| + |\mathcal{A}_1|)(|\mathcal{B}_0| + |\mathcal{B}_1|)$ equals $(|\mathcal{A}_0| - |\mathcal{A}_1|)(|\mathcal{B}_0| - |\mathcal{B}_1|)$. This is at least $0$ because $\mathcal{A}_1 \subseteq \mathcal{A}_0$ and $\mathcal{B}_1 \subseteq \mathcal{B}_0$. It is Chebyshev's sum inequality for two terms.

steps.slogan: Apply the induction hypothesis to the pairs $(\mathcal{A}_0, \mathcal{B}_0)$ and $(\mathcal{A}_1, \mathcal{B}_1)$.
steps.detail: Both pairs are lower families inside the power set of $S \setminus \{a\}$, which has $n - 1$ elements. So $|\mathcal{A}_i||\mathcal{B}_i| \le 2^{n-1}|\mathcal{A}_i \cap \mathcal{B}_i|$ for $i = 0, 1$.

steps.slogan: Recognize $|\mathcal{A}_0 \cap \mathcal{B}_0| + |\mathcal{A}_1 \cap \mathcal{B}_1|$ as $|\mathcal{A} \cap \mathcal{B}|$.
steps.detail: A set without $a$ lies in $\mathcal{A} \cap \mathcal{B}$ exactly when it lies in $\mathcal{A}_0 \cap \mathcal{B}_0$. A set $T \cup \{a\}$ lies in $\mathcal{A} \cap \mathcal{B}$ exactly when $T \in \mathcal{A}_1 \cap \mathcal{B}_1$. Chaining the bounds gives $|\mathcal{A}||\mathcal{B}| \le 2 \cdot 2^{n-1} |\mathcal{A} \cap \mathcal{B}|$.

concepts.c:lower-set: Lowness gives $\mathcal{A}_1 \subseteq \mathcal{A}_0$ and keeps both halves lower.
concepts.c:finite-set: Removing one element at a time reduces the finite ground set to the empty set.
concepts.c:family-of-sets: The theorem compares the sizes of two families of subsets.

source.note: mathlib proves the general form IsLowerSet.le_card_inter_finset' by Finset.induction on the ground set, splitting with memberSubfamily and nonMemberSubfamily and using mul_add_mul_le_mul_add_mul.

statement: A subset $S$ of [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space) $\mathbb{R}^n$ is [compact](c:compact-space) if and only if it is [closed](c:closed-set) and [bounded](c:bounded-set).

hypotheses.text: $S$ is a subset of [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space) $\mathbb{R}^n$ with its usual metric, where $n \ge 0$.

conclusion: $S$ is compact if and only if $S$ is closed and bounded.

formal.difference: The declaration holds in every proper metric space, one whose closed balls are compact. Euclidean space is proper by FiniteDimensional.proper.

proofs.name: Compact cube
proofs.slogan: Compact sets are closed and bounded in any metric space; conversely a bounded closed set is a closed subset of a compact cube.
proofs.scope: Both directions, for every $n \ge 0$ and including the empty set, for which every step is trivial. Only the converse uses the structure of $\mathbb{R}^n$.

roles.why: Inside $\mathbb{R}^n$ the balls and cubes are available, and the cube $[-r, r]^n$ is compact.

steps.slogan: Cover a compact $S$ by the balls $B(0, k)$ and keep finitely many.
steps.detail: The balls $B(0, k)$ for $k \in \mathbb{N}$ form an [open cover](c:open-cover) of $\mathbb{R}^n$. A finite subcover has a largest radius $K$, so $S \subseteq B(0, K)$ and $S$ is bounded.

steps.slogan: Separate each outside point from a compact $S$ by two disjoint balls.
steps.detail: Let $p \notin S$. For each $x \in S$ the balls $B(x, r_x)$ and $B(p, r_x)$ with $r_x = |x - p|/2$ are disjoint. Finitely many $B(x_i, r_{x_i})$ cover $S$, so $B(p, \min_i r_{x_i})$ misses $S$. Hence the complement of $S$ is open.

steps.slogan: Show that every closed interval $[-r, r]$ is compact.
steps.detail: Take an open cover. Let $s$ be the supremum of the $x \in [-r, r]$ for which $[-r, x]$ has a finite subcover. A member of the cover contains $(s - \delta, s + \delta)$, so a finite subcover reaches beyond $s$ unless $s = r$. Thus $s = r$ and $[-r, r]$ is covered.

steps.slogan: Show that the cube $[-r, r]^n$ is compact as a finite product of compact intervals.
steps.detail: A finite product of compact spaces is compact, by Tychonoff's theorem or by the tube lemma and induction on $n$. The product topology on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is the metric topology.

steps.slogan: Place a bounded closed $S$ in a cube and show that it is compact.
steps.detail: Boundedness gives $S \subseteq B(0, r) \subseteq [-r, r]^n$. Given an open cover of $S$, add the open set $\mathbb{R}^n \setminus S$; this covers the compact cube, so finitely many members cover it. Dropping $\mathbb{R}^n \setminus S$ leaves a finite subcover of $S$.

steps.slogan: Join both directions into the stated equivalence.
steps.detail: Compact implies bounded and closed by the first two steps. Bounded and closed implies compact by the last three steps.

concepts.c:euclidean-space: The cubes and balls of $\mathbb{R}^n$ carry the whole argument.
concepts.c:compact-space: Compactness is the finite subcover property that is proved or used.
concepts.c:closed-set: Closedness lets a subset of a compact cube inherit compactness.
concepts.c:bounded-set: Boundedness places the set inside one cube.
concepts.c:open-cover: Compactness is stated and used through open covers.

source.note: mathlib uses IsCompact.isClosed and IsCompact.isBounded, and isCompact_of_isClosed_isBounded: a bounded set lies in a closed ball, which is compact, and IsCompact.of_isClosed_subset follows.

statement: Let $T$ be a [linear map](c:linear-map) defined on all of a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $H$ that is [symmetric](c:symmetric-operator): $\langle Tx, y\rangle = \langle x, Ty\rangle$ for all $x, y \in H$. Then $T$ is a [bounded linear operator](c:bounded-linear-operator).

hypotheses.text: $H$ is a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space), complete, over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$.
$T \colon H \to H$ is a [linear map](c:linear-map) defined on all of $H$.
$T$ is [symmetric](c:symmetric-operator): $\langle Tx, y\rangle = \langle x, Ty\rangle$ for all $x, y$.

conclusion: There is $C$ with $\|Tx\| \le C\|x\|$ for all $x$, so $T$ is continuous.

formal.difference: The declaration concludes that $T$ is continuous, which is equivalent to boundedness for a linear map. It is stated for a complete inner product space over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$.

proofs.name: Closed graph
proofs.slogan: Show that the graph of $T$ is closed by moving $T$ across the inner product, then use the closed graph theorem.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. Sequences suffice to test closedness of the graph, because $H$ is a metric space.

roles.why: Completeness makes $H$ a [Banach space](c:banach-space), as the closed graph theorem needs, and the inner product is continuous.
Linearity gives $Tu_k - Tx = T(u_k - x)$ and makes the closed graph theorem apply.
Symmetry moves $T$ from the first slot of the inner product to the second.

steps.slogan: Reduce boundedness of $T$ to closedness of its graph.
steps.detail: The space $H$ is a [Banach space](c:banach-space). By the closed graph theorem, a [linear map](c:linear-map) $H \to H$ with closed graph is bounded. Closedness means: if $u_k \to x$ and $Tu_k \to y$, then $y = Tx$.

steps.slogan: Take a sequence $u_k \to x$ with $Tu_k \to y$ and set $z = y - Tx$.
steps.detail: The goal is $z = 0$. We show $\|z\|^2 = 0$.

steps.slogan: Move $T$ across the inner product to get $\langle Tu_k - Tx, z \rangle = \langle u_k - x, Tz \rangle$.
steps.detail: Linearity gives $Tu_k - Tx = T(u_k - x)$. [Symmetry](c:symmetric-operator) of $T$ then gives $\langle T(u_k - x), z\rangle = \langle u_k - x, Tz\rangle$.

steps.slogan: Let $k \to \infty$ on both sides of the identity.
steps.detail: The inner product is continuous. The left side tends to $\langle y - Tx, z\rangle = \|z\|^2$. The right side tends to $\langle 0, Tz\rangle = 0$, because $u_k - x \to 0$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $y = Tx$, so the graph is closed and $T$ is bounded.
steps.detail: The two limits are equal, so $\|z\|^2 = 0$ and $y = Tx$. The graph is closed, and step 1 makes $T$ [bounded](c:bounded-linear-operator).

concepts.c:hilbert-space: Its completeness and inner product drive both the closed graph theorem and the limit.
concepts.c:linear-map: Linearity of $T$ is used to split $Tu_k - Tx$ and to apply the theorem.
concepts.c:symmetric-operator: Symmetry transfers $T$ across the inner product.
concepts.c:bounded-linear-operator: Boundedness is the conclusion given by the closed graph theorem.
concepts.c:banach-space: The closed graph theorem needs a complete normed domain and codomain.

source.note: mathlib uses LinearMap.continuous_of_seq_closed_graph (the closed graph theorem), the identity ⟪Tu_k - Tx, y - Tx⟫ = ⟪u_k - x, T(y - Tx)⟫, and Filter.Tendsto.inner with inner_self_eq_zero.

statement: A [triangle](c:triangle) with side lengths $a, b, c$ and semiperimeter $s = (a+b+c)/2$ has [area](c:area) $\sqrt{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}$.

hypotheses.text: The numbers $a, b, c$ are the side lengths of a nondegenerate [triangle](c:triangle).

proofs.name: Law of cosines
proofs.slogan: Write the area as $\tfrac12 ab \sin C$, get $\cos C$ from the law of cosines, and factor $16\,\mathrm{Area}^2$ with difference of squares.
proofs.scope: The whole formula, with $C$ the angle between sides $a$ and $b$. The angle $C$ lies strictly between $0$ and $\pi$, so $\sin C > 0$.

roles.why: A nondegenerate triangle gives $0 < C < \pi$, so $\sin C > 0$ and the four factors are positive.

steps.slogan: Write the [area](c:area) as $\tfrac12 ab \sin C$.
steps.detail: Take $b$ as the base. The height is $a \sin C$, with $C$ the angle between $a$ and $b$. So the area is $\tfrac12 ab \sin C$, and $\sin C > 0$.

steps.slogan: Express $\cos C$ through the sides by the law of cosines.
steps.detail: The [cosine](c:cosine) satisfies $c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos C$, so $2ab\cos C = a^2 + b^2 - c^2$.

steps.slogan: Square the area and replace $\sin^2 C$ by $1 - \cos^2 C$.
Factor the difference of squares twice.
Rewrite the four factors with $s$ and take the square root.
steps.detail: We have $a+b+c = 2s$, $a+b-c = 2(s-c)$, $a-b+c = 2(s-b)$ and $-a+b+c = 2(s-a)$. So $16\,\mathrm{Area}^2 = 16\,s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)$. The area is positive, so it is the positive square root.

concepts.c:triangle: The sides and angles of a triangle are the data of the formula.
concepts.c:area: The area is the quantity that the formula computes.
concepts.c:cosine: The cosine of the angle $C$ links the three side lengths.

source.note: The standard derivation from the law of cosines and a double difference of squares.

statement: Let $\lambda$ be a [partition](c:integer-partition) of $n$ with [Young diagram](c:young-diagram) of $n$ cells. The number $f^\lambda$ of [standard Young tableaux](c:standard-young-tableau) of shape $\lambda$ equals $n! / \prod_{c \in \lambda} h(c)$. The hook length $h(c)$ counts the cell $c$, the cells to its right in its row and the cells below it in its column.

hypotheses.text: $\lambda$ is a [partition](c:integer-partition) of $n \ge 0$ drawn as a [Young diagram](c:young-diagram) of $n$ cells.

proofs.name: Hook walk
proofs.slogan: The recurrence $f^\lambda = \sum_c f^{\lambda - c}$ holds for the hook-length expression because the probabilities of the hook walk ending at the corners sum to one.
proofs.scope: All partitions, by induction on $n$ with $F(\emptyset) = 1$ for the empty partition. The probability identity is proved for a fixed partition $\lambda$ with $n \ge 1$.

roles.why: The diagram has corner cells, which give the recurrence, and its hooks define the walk.

steps.slogan: Remove the cell holding $n$ to get $f^\lambda = \sum_c f^{\lambda - c}$.
steps.detail: In a [standard Young tableau](c:standard-young-tableau) of shape $\lambda$ the entry $n$ sits in a corner cell $c$. Deleting it leaves a standard tableau of shape $\lambda - c$, and every such tableau arises from one corner. So $f^\lambda = \sum_{c\ \mathrm{corner}} f^{\lambda - c}$, with $f^\emptyset = 1$.

steps.slogan: Reduce the formula to a ratio identity for $F(\lambda) = n!/\prod h(c)$.
steps.detail: By induction on $n$ it suffices that $F$ satisfies $F(\lambda) = \sum_c F(\lambda - c)$ and $F(\emptyset) = 1$. Removing the corner $(a, b)$ changes only the hooks in its row and column, so $F(\lambda - c)/F(\lambda) = \frac1n \prod_{i<a} \frac{h_{ib}}{h_{ib} - 1} \prod_{j<b} \frac{h_{aj}}{h_{aj} - 1}$. It remains to show that these ratios add up to $1$.

steps.slogan: Define the hook walk: jump from a uniform random cell to a uniform random other cell of the current hook.
steps.detail: Start at a uniformly random cell of $\lambda$ and repeat: move to a uniformly random other cell in the hook of the current cell. The hook shrinks each time, so the walk stops at a corner. Hence the probabilities $p(c)$ of ending at the corners sum to $1$.

steps.slogan: Show that the walk ends at the corner $c$ with probability $F(\lambda - c)/F(\lambda)$.
steps.detail: Fix the corner $(a, b)$. By induction on the number of visited rows and columns, the walk with row set $I$ and column set $J$ above and left of $c$ has probability $\frac1n \prod_{i \in I}\frac{1}{h_{ib}-1}\prod_{j \in J}\frac{1}{h_{aj}-1}$. Summing over all $I, J$ gives $\frac1n \prod_{i<a}\bigl(1 + \frac{1}{h_{ib}-1}\bigr)\prod_{j<b}\bigl(1 + \frac{1}{h_{aj}-1}\bigr) = F(\lambda - c)/F(\lambda)$.

steps.slogan: Combine the identity with the recurrence by induction on $n$.
steps.detail: The two previous steps give $\sum_c F(\lambda - c)/F(\lambda) = \sum_c p(c) = 1$, so $F$ satisfies the recurrence of $f$. With $F(\emptyset) = f^\emptyset = 1$, induction on $n$ gives $F = f^\lambda$.

concepts.c:integer-partition: The shape $\lambda$ is a partition of $n$.
concepts.c:young-diagram: Corner cells and hooks of the diagram drive the recurrence and the walk.
concepts.c:standard-young-tableau: The count $f^\lambda$ of these tableaux is the quantity computed.

source.note: Greene, Nijenhuis and Wilf, A probabilistic proof of a formula for the number of Young tableaux of a given shape, Advances in Mathematics 31 (1979), 104-109: the hook walk.

statement: Let $f \colon X \to E$ be [integrable](c:integrable-function) with values in a normed space, and let $g \colon X \to \mathbb{K}$ be measurable with finite [essential supremum](c:essential-supremum) $\|g\|_\infty$ of $|g|$. Then $gf$ is integrable and $\int \|gf\|\, d\mu \le \|g\|_\infty \int \|f\|\, d\mu$.

hypotheses.text: $f \colon X \to E$ is [integrable](c:integrable-function) for the measure $\mu$.
$g \colon X \to \mathbb{K}$ is a [measurable function](c:measurable-function), where $\mathbb{K}$ is $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$.
The [essential supremum](c:essential-supremum) $M = \|g\|_\infty$ of $|g|$ is finite.

conclusion: The product $gf$ is integrable and $\int \|gf\|\, d\mu \le \|g\|_\infty \int \|f\|\, d\mu$.

formal.difference: The declaration proves integrability of $g \cdot f$ only, for scalars in a normed ring acting boundedly on the codomain. The norm bound is the eLpNorm inequality used inside its proof.

proofs.name: Essential bound and monotonicity
proofs.slogan: Bound $\|gf\|$ by $M\|f\|$ almost everywhere, then integrate the bound with the monotone [Lebesgue integral](c:lebesgue-integral).
proofs.scope: The whole statement; this is Hölder's inequality with exponents $\infty$ and $1$. Null sets are ignored throughout.

roles.why: A finite essential supremum gives the almost-everywhere bound $|g| \le M$.
Measurability of $g$ makes $gf$ measurable, so the integral of $\|gf\|$ is defined.
Integrability of $f$ makes $M \int \|f\|$ finite.

steps.slogan: Show that $|g| \le M$ almost everywhere.
steps.detail: $M$ is the infimum of the $c$ with $\mu(|g| > c) = 0$. The set $\{|g| > M\}$ equals $\bigcup_n \{|g| > M + 1/n\}$, a countable union of null sets. So it is null.

steps.slogan: Bound $\|g(x)f(x)\|$ by $M\|f(x)\|$ at almost every point.
steps.detail: We have $\|g(x) f(x)\| = |g(x)|\,\|f(x)\|$. Outside the null set of the previous step this is at most $M\|f(x)\|$.

steps.slogan: Check that $gf$ is measurable.
steps.detail: The product of an almost everywhere measurable scalar function and an almost everywhere strongly measurable function is almost everywhere strongly measurable, as a limit of products of simple functions.

steps.slogan: Integrate the pointwise bound to get $\int \|gf\| \le M \int \|f\|$.
steps.detail: The [Lebesgue integral](c:lebesgue-integral) is monotone on nonnegative functions, so $\int \|gf\|\,d\mu \le M\int \|f\|\,d\mu$. This is finite because $f$ is integrable. With measurability, $gf$ is integrable.

concepts.c:integrable-function: Integrability of $f$ gives a finite bound for $gf$.
concepts.c:essential-supremum: The essential supremum is the almost-everywhere bound on $|g|$.
concepts.c:measurable-function: Measurability is needed for $gf$ to have an integral at all.
concepts.c:lebesgue-integral: Monotonicity of the integral turns the pointwise bound into an integral bound.

statement: Let $n \ge 1$. Every [continuous](c:continuous-function) $f \colon [0,1]^n \to \mathbb{R}$ is a [superposition](c:superposition) $f(x) = \sum_{q=0}^{2n} \Phi_q\bigl(\sum_{p=1}^{n} \varphi_{q,p}(x_p)\bigr)$ of continuous functions of one variable. The inner functions $\varphi_{q,p}$ do not depend on $f$.

hypotheses.text: $n \ge 1$ is an integer.
$f$ is a [continuous function](c:continuous-function) on the cube $[0,1]^n$.

conclusion: There are continuous inner functions $\varphi_{q,p}$, fixed in advance, and continuous outer functions $\Phi_q$ depending on $f$, with $f(x) = \sum_{q=0}^{2n}\Phi_q\bigl(\sum_p \varphi_{q,p}(x_p)\bigr)$.

proofs.name: Universal inner functions and iteration
proofs.slogan: Fix universal inner functions that separate small cubes in $2n+1$ families, approximate any continuous function by outer functions to a fixed fraction of its norm, and iterate.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof; the construction of the inner functions and the approximation lemma rest on the cited work. The inner functions are built before $f$ is given.

roles.why: The dimension $n$ fixes the number $2n+1$ of families of cubes and of outer functions.
Continuity of $f$ on the compact cube gives small oscillation on small cubes and a bounded norm.

steps.slogan: Construct fixed continuous inner functions that separate small cubes in $2n+1$ families.
steps.detail: For $q = 0, \dots, 2n$ the cited proof builds continuous $\varphi_{q,p}$ and sums $\xi_q(x) = \sum_p \varphi_{q,p}(x_p)$. At every scale the cubes of one family have disjoint images under $\xi_q$, and every point lies in the cubes of at least $n+1$ families. This does not depend on $f$.

steps.slogan: Approximate a continuous function $g$ by $\sum_q \Phi_q \circ \xi_q$ up to a fixed fraction of $\|g\|$.
steps.detail: Choose a scale where $g$ varies little on each cube. Define $\Phi_q$ on the disjoint image intervals as the value of $g$ at a cube center, divided by $n+1$. At each point at least $n+1$ families contribute correctly, so $\|g - \sum_q \Phi_q\circ\xi_q\| \le \theta\|g\|$ for a constant $\theta < 1$, and $\|\Phi_q\| \le \|g\|$.

steps.slogan: Apply the approximation again to each remainder $f_m$.
steps.detail: Put $f_0 = f$ and $f_{m+1} = f_m - \sum_q \Phi_q^{(m)} \circ \xi_q$. Then $\|f_m\| \le \theta^m\|f\|$ and $\|\Phi_q^{(m)}\| \le \theta^m \|f\|$.

steps.slogan: Sum the outer functions and show that the series converges uniformly to $f$.
steps.detail: The series $\Phi_q = \sum_m \Phi_q^{(m)}$ converges uniformly, because the terms decrease geometrically, so $\Phi_q$ is continuous. Telescoping gives $\sum_q \Phi_q\circ\xi_q = \sum_m (f_m - f_{m+1}) = f - \lim f_m = f$.

concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity gives small oscillation on small cubes and keeps the series continuous.
concepts.c:superposition: The theorem writes $f$ as a superposition of one-variable functions and addition.

source.ref: A. N. Kolmogorov, On the representation of continuous functions of several variables by superposition of continuous functions of one variable and addition, Dokl. Akad. Nauk SSSR 114 (1957), 953-956
source.note: The steps follow the streamlined proofs in G. G. Lorentz, Approximation of Functions, Holt, Rinehart and Winston, 1966, and J.-P. Kahane, Sur le theoreme de superposition de Kolmogorov, J. Approx. Theory 13 (1975), 229-234.

statement: Let $h(I)$ be a nondegenerate real-analytic [integrable system](c:integrable-system) and $\varepsilon f$ a small analytic perturbation. Each invariant torus of $h$ with [Diophantine](c:diophantine-condition) frequency $\omega$ persists, slightly deformed, as an invariant torus of $h + \varepsilon f$ with the same frequency. These tori fill all of phase space except a set whose measure tends to $0$ with $\gamma$.

hypotheses.text: $H_0 = h(I)$ is a real-analytic [integrable system](c:integrable-system) in action-angle variables on $D \times \mathbb{T}^n$.
The frequency map $I \mapsto \nabla h(I)$ is nondegenerate: $\det \partial^2 h \ne 0$.
The perturbation $\varepsilon f$ is real analytic and $|\varepsilon|$ is small, depending on $\gamma$ and $\tau$.
The torus has frequency $\omega$ with $|k \cdot \omega| \ge \gamma |k|^{-\tau}$ for all $k \in \mathbb{Z}^n \setminus \{0\}$, where $\tau > n - 1$.

conclusion: The torus persists as a deformed analytic invariant torus of $h + \varepsilon f$ with frequency $\omega$, and the measure of the phase-space complement of all persisting tori tends to $0$ as $\gamma \to 0$.

proofs.name: Newton iteration on a normal form
proofs.slogan: Put the Hamiltonian near the torus in Kolmogorov normal form, remove the perturbation by a rapidly converging Newton scheme, and count the admissible frequencies.
proofs.scope: An outline of the analytic KAM proof of Pöschel; the estimates for the small divisors and the convergence rest on the cited work. Real-analytic Hamiltonians only; finite smoothness needs other work.

roles.why: Action-angle variables make the unperturbed torus $I = I_0$ carry a linear flow with frequency $\omega$.
Invertibility of $\partial^2 h$ fixes the frequency in each step and makes the frequency map a local diffeomorphism.
Smallness of the analytic perturbation makes the Newton steps contract.
The Diophantine bound controls the small divisors $1/(k \cdot \omega)$ in the linear equation.

steps.slogan: Bring the Hamiltonian near the chosen torus into Kolmogorov normal form.
steps.detail: Take the action $I_0$ with $\nabla h(I_0) = \omega$ and put $y = I - I_0$. Then $H = e + \omega \cdot y + \tfrac12 A y \cdot y + \dots + \varepsilon f$, where $A = \partial^2 h(I_0)$ is invertible by nondegeneracy. The torus $y = 0$ is invariant for the unperturbed part.

steps.slogan: Solve the linearized equation on the torus by Fourier series.
steps.detail: The step needs $\omega \cdot \partial_x F = f - [f]$. The Fourier coefficients are $f_k / (i\, k \cdot \omega)$, and the Diophantine bound gives $|k \cdot \omega|^{-1} \le |k|^\tau/\gamma$. Analyticity gives exponentially decaying coefficients, so $F$ is analytic on a slightly smaller strip.

steps.slogan: Conjugate by the symplectic map generated by $F$ to get a quadratically smaller perturbation.
steps.detail: The flow of $F$ removes the order $\varepsilon$ terms that do not depend on $y$. A translation of $y$ by $O(\varepsilon)$, solved with the invertible $A$, removes the average term linear in $y$ and keeps the frequency $\omega$. Cauchy estimates bound the new perturbation by about $\varepsilon^2$, with constants depending on $\gamma$ and $\tau$.

steps.slogan: Iterate with shrinking strips and let the quadratic decay beat the loss of domain.
steps.detail: The errors satisfy $\varepsilon_{j+1} \lesssim \varepsilon_j^2$ while the strip widths shrink only geometrically. The composed symplectic maps converge to an analytic map. It sends $y = 0$ to an invariant torus of $H$ carrying a flow of frequency $\omega$.

steps.slogan: Count the Diophantine frequencies by nondegeneracy and estimate the missing measure.
steps.detail: The frequency map is a local diffeomorphism, so the frequencies that fail the Diophantine bound form a set of measure $O(\gamma)$. Each good frequency gives a persisting torus close to the unperturbed one, so the complement of the persisting tori has measure tending to $0$ with $\gamma$.

concepts.c:integrable-system: The unperturbed system supplies the tori that the theorem preserves.
concepts.c:diophantine-condition: It bounds the small divisors and defines the admissible frequencies.

source.ref: J. Pöschel, A lecture on the classical KAM theorem, in Smooth ergodic theory and its applications, Proc. Sympos. Pure Math. 69, Amer. Math. Soc., 2001, pp. 707-732
source.note: Pöschel's lecture gives a complete proof of Kolmogorov's theorem and of the measure estimate; the five steps follow it.

statement: Let $\mathcal{A}$ be a [family of sets](c:family-of-sets) of $r$-element subsets of $\{1, \dots, n\}$. Let $\mathcal{C}$ be an initial segment of the [colex order](c:colex-order) on $r$-sets with $|\mathcal{C}| \le |\mathcal{A}|$. Then the [shadow](c:shadow) of $\mathcal{C}$ is no larger than the shadow of $\mathcal{A}$: $|\partial \mathcal{C}| \le |\partial \mathcal{A}|$.

hypotheses.text: $\mathcal{A}$ is a [family of sets](c:family-of-sets), each an $r$-element subset of $\{1, \dots, n\}$.
$\mathcal{C}$ is an initial segment of the [colex order](c:colex-order) on $r$-sets, with $|\mathcal{C}| \le |\mathcal{A}|$.

conclusion: The [shadow](c:shadow) satisfies $|\partial \mathcal{C}| \le |\partial \mathcal{A}|$, so initial segments of colex have the smallest shadows.

formal.difference: The catalog title also covers the characterization of $f$-vectors of simplicial complexes through cascade representations. The declaration proves only the shadow-minimization form stated here.

proofs.name: Compression to an initial segment
proofs.slogan: Compress the family step by step, never increasing its shadow, until it is a colex initial segment, then compare it with $\mathcal{C}$.
proofs.scope: All $r$ and $n$. A compression $C_{U,V}$ needs disjoint $U, V$ of the same size with $\max U < \max V$; a trivial compression changes nothing.

roles.why: Uniform size $r$ is kept by every compression and defines the shadow.
The size bound lets us shrink $\mathcal{A}$ to the size of $\mathcal{C}$, and initial segments of equal size coincide.

steps.slogan: Replace $\mathcal{A}$ by a subfamily $\mathcal{A}'$ with $|\mathcal{A}'| = |\mathcal{C}|$.
steps.detail: A subfamily has a smaller shadow, so $|\partial \mathcal{A}'| \le |\partial \mathcal{A}|$. It suffices to prove $|\partial \mathcal{C}| \le |\partial \mathcal{A}'|$ for families of equal size.

steps.slogan: Define the compression $C_{U,V}$ for disjoint $U, V$ with $|U| = |V|$ and $\max U < \max V$.
steps.detail: Replace each member $A$ with $V \subseteq A$ and $A \cap U = \emptyset$ by $(A \setminus V) \cup U$, unless that set is already in the family. The size of the family and the size $r$ of the sets stay the same. A moved set is smaller in the [colex order](c:colex-order) because $\max U < \max V$.

steps.slogan: Show that a compression never increases the shadow when all smaller compressions are already done.
steps.detail: Assume that the family is invariant under every compression $C_{U',V'}$ with $|U'| < |U|$. Then for each $x \in U$ the pair $(U \setminus \{x\}, V \setminus \{\min V\})$ leaves the family unchanged. This gives $|\partial\, C_{U,V}(\mathcal{A})| \le |\partial \mathcal{A}|$.

steps.slogan: Compress repeatedly until no useful compression changes the family.
steps.detail: Take the useful compression with the smallest $|U|$ that changes the family. It strictly lowers the natural number $\sum_{A}\sum_{a \in A} 2^a$, so the process stops at a family $\mathcal{B}$. Then $|\mathcal{B}| = |\mathcal{A}'|$, $\mathcal{B}$ is $r$-uniform, $|\partial\mathcal{B}| \le |\partial\mathcal{A}'|$, and every useful compression leaves $\mathcal{B}$ unchanged.

steps.slogan: Show that a family unchanged by all useful compressions is a colex initial segment.
steps.detail: Suppose $A \in \mathcal{B}$, $A' \notin \mathcal{B}$, $|A'| = r$ and $A' <_{\mathrm{colex}} A$. Put $U = A' \setminus A$ and $V = A \setminus A'$; then $\max U < \max V$. The compression $C_{U,V}$ moves $A$ to $A'$ and so changes $\mathcal{B}$, a contradiction.

steps.slogan: Compare the initial segments $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ of equal size.
steps.detail: Initial segments of the colex order are nested, so one contains the other. They have the same size, so $\mathcal{B} = \mathcal{C}$. Hence $|\partial \mathcal{C}| = |\partial \mathcal{B}| \le |\partial \mathcal{A}'| \le |\partial \mathcal{A}|$.

concepts.c:family-of-sets: The theorem concerns families of $r$-element sets and their sizes.
concepts.c:colex-order: Compressions lower sets in colex, and the extremal families are colex initial segments.
concepts.c:shadow: The shadow is the quantity that compressions never increase.

source.note: mathlib takes a subfamily of equal size (exists_subset_card_eq), compresses with UV.kruskal_katona_helper (compression_improved, familyMeasure), uses UV.isInitSeg_of_compressed and IsInitSeg.total.

statement: In a [triangle](c:triangle) with sides $a, b, c$ opposite the angles $A, B, C$, we have $\dfrac{a}{\sin A} = \dfrac{b}{\sin B} = \dfrac{c}{\sin C}$, with the [sine function](c:sine-function).

hypotheses.text: Three non-collinear points of a Euclidean space form a [triangle](c:triangle) with sides $a, b, c$ opposite the angles $A, B, C$.

formal.difference: The declaration states $\sin\angle p_1p_2p_3 \cdot |p_2p_3| = \sin\angle p_3p_1p_2 \cdot |p_3p_1|$ for any three points, collinear or not. The ratio form follows by dividing by nonzero sines and sides.

proofs.name: Gram expression
proofs.slogan: Write $\sin\theta \cdot \|u\|\|v\|$ as the square root of a Gram determinant, show that it is the same at every vertex, and divide.
proofs.scope: Nondegenerate triangles in any real inner product space. The sines and side lengths are positive, so the divisions are allowed.

roles.why: Non-collinear points give positive sides and angles strictly between $0$ and $\pi$, so every sine is positive.

steps.slogan: Write $\sin\theta\,\|u\|\|v\|$ as $G(u, v) = \sqrt{\|u\|^2\|v\|^2 - \langle u, v\rangle^2}$.
steps.detail: For the angle $\theta$ between nonzero vectors $u, v$ of an [inner product space](c:inner-product-space) we have $\cos\theta\,\|u\|\|v\| = \langle u, v\rangle$. Since $\sin\theta \ge 0$ and $\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1$, we get $\sin\theta\,\|u\|\|v\| = G(u, v)$.

steps.slogan: Show that $G(u, v) = G(v, u - v)$.
steps.detail: Expand $\|v\|^2\|u - v\|^2 - \langle v, u - v\rangle^2 = \|v\|^2(\|u\|^2 - 2\langle u, v\rangle + \|v\|^2) - (\langle u, v\rangle - \|v\|^2)^2$. The terms in $\langle u, v\rangle\|v\|^2$ and $\|v\|^4$ cancel, leaving $\|u\|^2\|v\|^2 - \langle u, v\rangle^2$.

steps.slogan: Carry $G$ from vertex to vertex along the triangle.
steps.detail: $G$ is unchanged by swapping its arguments and by a sign change of either. The third side vector is the difference of the two sides at a vertex, so the previous step moves $G$ to the next vertex. With the first step this gives $\sin A \cdot bc = \sin B \cdot ca = \sin C \cdot ab$.

steps.slogan: Divide by $abc$ and invert to get the ratios.
steps.detail: The product $abc$ is positive for a triangle. Division gives $\sin A / a = \sin B / b = \sin C / c$. All sines are positive, so inversion gives $a/\sin A = b/\sin B = c/\sin C$.

concepts.c:triangle: Its three vertices carry the same Gram expression.
concepts.c:sine-function: The sines of the angles are the quantities that the law compares.
concepts.c:inner-product-space: The angle and the Gram expression come from the inner product.

source.note: mathlib proves InnerProductGeometry.sin_angle_mul_norm_eq_sin_angle_mul_norm by writing sin(angle x y) with √(⟪x,x⟫⟪y,y⟫ - ⟪x,y⟫²) and comparing two such expressions; the point form adds angle_comm and angle_neg_right.

statement: Let $X$ be a [random variable](c:random-variable) with [density](c:probability-density-function) $p$ with respect to a measure $\mu$ on its target. If $f$ is measurable and $f(X)$ is integrable, then $f p$ is $\mu$-integrable and the [expected value](c:expected-value) is $\mathbb{E}[f(X)] = \int f(x)\, p(x)\, d\mu(x)$.

hypotheses.text: $X$ is a measurable map from a probability space $(\Omega, P)$ to a measurable space $(E, \mathcal{E})$, a [random variable](c:random-variable).
$X$ has [density](c:probability-density-function) $p \ge 0$ with respect to $\mu$: $P(X \in A) = \int_A p\, d\mu$ for every measurable $A$.
$f \colon E \to \mathbb{R}$ is a [measurable function](c:measurable-function), and $f(X)$ is integrable.

conclusion: The function $fp$ is $\mu$-integrable and $\mathbb{E}[f(X)] = \int f p\, d\mu$.

formal.difference: The declaration allows values of $f$ in a Banach space, with $f$ only almost everywhere strongly measurable for $\mu$, and defines the density as the Radon-Nikodym derivative of the law of $X$. It needs no integrability hypothesis, because the Bochner integral of a non-integrable function is $0$.

proofs.name: Law and density
proofs.slogan: Rewrite the expectation as an integral against the law of $X$, replace the law by the measure $p\mu$, and integrate against that measure.
proofs.scope: Real-valued $f$. Both change-of-variable steps are proved for indicators, then simple functions, nonnegative functions, and integrable functions.

roles.why: Measurability of $X$ defines its law, the [pushforward measure](c:pushforward-measure) of $P$.
The density identity says that the law of $X$ equals the measure $p\mu$.
Measurability and integrability let us split $f = f^+ - f^-$ and pass to the limit.

steps.slogan: Write $\mathbb{E}[f(X)]$ as the integral of $f$ against the law $P_X$ of $X$.
steps.detail: The law $P_X(A) = P(X \in A)$ is the [pushforward measure](c:pushforward-measure) of $P$ by $X$. For $f = 1_A$ the identity $\int f(X)\, dP = \int f\, dP_X$ is the definition of $P_X$. Linearity gives simple functions, monotone convergence gives nonnegative ones, and $f = f^+ - f^-$ gives the integrable case.

steps.slogan: Identify the law $P_X$ with the measure $p\mu$ with density $p$.
steps.detail: The hypothesis gives $P_X(A) = \int_A p\, d\mu = (p\mu)(A)$ for every measurable $A$. So $P_X = p\mu$ as measures. Such a $p$ is the [Radon-Nikodym derivative](c:radon-nikodym-derivative) of $P_X$ with respect to $\mu$ when $P_X \ll \mu$.

steps.slogan: Show that integrating against $p\mu$ equals integrating $fp$ against $\mu$.
steps.detail: For $f = 1_A$ both sides equal $\int_A p\, d\mu$. Linearity, monotone convergence and the split $f = f^+ - f^-$ extend this to all measurable $f$, for which either side exists.

steps.slogan: Chain the equalities and transfer integrability.
steps.detail: We get $\mathbb{E}[f(X)] = \int f\, dP_X = \int f\, d(p\mu) = \int f p\, d\mu$. The same chain for $|f|$ gives $\int |f| p\, d\mu = \mathbb{E}|f(X)| < \infty$, so $fp$ is integrable.

concepts.c:random-variable: Its law is the measure that carries the expectation.
concepts.c:probability-density-function: The density is the weight that turns the law into $p\mu$.
concepts.c:expected-value: The expected value is the quantity that the formula computes.
concepts.c:pushforward-measure: The law of $X$ is the pushforward of $P$.
concepts.c:radon-nikodym-derivative: The density is the Radon-Nikodym derivative of the law.
concepts.c:measurable-function: Measurability of $f$ makes both integrals defined.
